Content:
Just as we can form partitions of closed intervals of the real line, we can also partition rectangular regions in the Cartesian plane.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the rectangle [MATH: R,] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f0a1ea7c7a6bbe9b9462a744f63a9458]

Content:
We can describe the entire rectange as [MATH: R = [1,4]\times [2,4],] where [MATH: \times] denotes the Cartesian product.

Content:
Now, let's partition [MATH: R] into [MATH: 6] rectangles of equal area, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/545bb9800ad27a7a6d0d7a6b3f40a422]

Content:
Note that we can describe our partition without a diagram as follows:

Content:
- The partition of the [MATH: x]-interval [MATH: [1,4]] can be expressed as [MATH: P_1 = \{1,2,3,4\},] where [MATH: x_0=1,] [MATH: x_1=2,] [MATH: x_2=3,] and [MATH: x_3=4.]
- The partition of the [MATH: y]-interval [MATH: [2,4]] can be expressed as [MATH: P_2 = \{2,3,4\},] where [MATH: y_0=2,] [MATH: y_1=3,] and [MATH: y_2=4.]
- The partition of the entire rectangle can be described as [MATH: P = P_1\times P_2.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
We have our partition [MATH: P = P_1\times P_2,] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6faf86c2f1962249a5b41df8627b3b2d]

Content:
Let [MATH: \Delta x_i] be the difference in the [MATH: x]-values of any two successive points in [MATH: P_1 = \{x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3\}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}]

Content:
Similarly, let [MATH: \Delta y_j] be the difference in the [MATH: y]-values of any two successive points in [MATH: P_2= \{y_0, y_1, y_2\}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}]

Content:
It turns out that evaluating double sums over rectangular partitions is important in some parts of higher-level math. For example, how do we compute the sum below?

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j]

Content:
First, note that we can use the product rule for double summations to write this sum as a product of two separate sums:

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j = \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j]

Content:
Now, recall that for partitions of intervals, the sum of differences in successive points is equal to the length of the interval.

Content:
- Here, the [MATH: x_i]'s partition the interval [MATH: [1,4]] which has length [MATH: 4 - 1 = 3.] So, we have [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^3 \Delta{x}_i = 3.]
- Similarly, the [MATH: y_j]'s partition the interval [MATH: [2,4]] which has length [MATH: 4 - 2 = 2.] So, we have [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^2 \Delta{y}_j = 2.]

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that

Content:
[MATH: ∑_(i = 1)^(m)∑_(j = 1)^(n)Δx_{i}Δy_{j}|= ∑_(i = 1)^(m)Δx_{i} ⋅ ∑_(j = 1)^(n)Δy_{j}; = 3 ⋅ 2; = 6.]

Content:
Note: There is plenty of geometric intuition here.

Content:
- [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i = 3] represents the width of the rectangle, while [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j = 2] represents the height.
- [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j] represents the area of the rectangle.

items.title: Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the following partitions:

  • [MATH: P_1 = \left\{x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_m\right\}] is a partition of the interval [MATH: [-1, 2]]

  • [MATH: P_2 = \left\{y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_n\right\}] is a partition of the interval [MATH: [2, 3]]

Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n {3} \Delta x_i \Delta y_j,] where [MATH: \Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}] and [MATH: \Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}.]
sections.readable_text:
Consider the following partitions:

- [MATH: P_1 = \left\{x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_m\right\}] is a partition of the interval [MATH: [-1, 2]]
- [MATH: P_2 = \left\{y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_n\right\}] is a partition of the interval [MATH: [2, 3]]

Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n {3} \Delta x_i \Delta y_j,] where [MATH: \Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}] and [MATH: \Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Using the constant multiple and product rules, we can write the summation as

[MATH: ∑_(i = 1)^(m)∑_(j = 1)^(n)3Δx_{i}Δy_{j}|= 3∑_(i = 1)^(m)∑_(j = 1)^(n)Δx_{i}Δy_{j}; = 3∑_(i = 1)^(m)Δx_{i}∑_(j = 1)^(n)Δy_{j}.]

Note that [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\Delta x_i] and [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j] are just the lengths of the intervals [MATH: [-1, 2]] and [MATH: [2,3]] respectively. So, we have

[MATH: ∑_(i = 1)^(m)Δx_{i}|= 2 − (− 1) = 3,; ∑_(j = 1)^(n)Δy_{j}|= 3 − 2 = 1.]

Combining our results, we have

[MATH: 3 \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j = 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 1 = 9.]

items.title: Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition Using a Difference of Squares

sections.normalized_html:
Consider the following partitions:

  • [MATH: P_1 = \left\{x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_m\right\}] is a partition of the interval [MATH: [4, 6]]

  • [MATH: P_2 = \left\{y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_n\right\}] is a partition of the interval [MATH: [2, 6]]

Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n (x_i + x_{i-1})\Delta x_i \Delta y_j,] where [MATH: \Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}] and [MATH: \Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}.]
sections.readable_text:
Consider the following partitions:

- [MATH: P_1 = \left\{x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_m\right\}] is a partition of the interval [MATH: [4, 6]]
- [MATH: P_2 = \left\{y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_n\right\}] is a partition of the interval [MATH: [2, 6]]

Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n (x_i + x_{i-1})\Delta x_i \Delta y_j,] where [MATH: \Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}] and [MATH: \Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Using the product rule, we can write the summation as

[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^m (x_i + x_{i-1})\Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j.]

Note that [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j] is just the length of the interval [MATH: [2, 6].] So, we have

[MATH: ∑_(j = 1)^(n)Δy_{j} = 6 − 2 = 4.]

For the sum over [MATH: i,] we can evaluate it as follows:

[MATH: ∑_(i = 1)^(m)(x_{i} + x_{i − 1})Δx_{i}|= (x_{1} + x_{0})Δx_{1} + (x_{2} + x_{1})Δx_{2} + ⋯ + (x_{m} + x_{m − 1})Δx_{n}; = (x_{1} + x_{0})(x_{1} − x_{0}) + (x_{2} + x_{1})(x_{2} − x_{1}) + (x_{m} + x_{m − 1})(x_{m} − x_{m − 1}); = (x_{1}^{2} − x_{0}^{2}) + (x_{2}^{2} − x_{1}^{2}) + ⋯ + (x_{m}^{2} − x_{m − 1}^{2}); = (x_{1}^{2} − x_{0}^{2}) + (x_{2}^{2} − x_{1}^{2}) + ⋯ + (x_{m}^{2} − x_{m − 1}^{2}); = − x_{0}^{2} + x_{m}^{2}; = x_{m}^{2} − x_{0}^{2}; = 6^{2} − 4^{2}; = 20] Combining our results, we finally arrive at [MATH: \sum_{i=1}^m (x_i + x_{i-1})\Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j = 20\cdot 4 = 80.]

Note that [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j] is just the length of the interval [MATH: [2, 6].] So, we have

[MATH: ∑_(j = 1)^(n)Δy_{j} = 6 − 2 = 4.]

Note that [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j] is just the length of the interval [MATH: [2, 6].] So, we have

[MATH: ∑_(j = 1)^(n)Δy_{j} = 6 − 2 = 4.]

For the sum over [MATH: i,] we can evaluate it as follows:

Combining our results, we finally arrive at
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^m (x_i + x_{i-1})\Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j = 20\cdot 4 = 80.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Just as we can form partitions of closed intervals of the real line, we can also partition rectangular regions in the Cartesian plane.

Content:
To demonstrate, consider the rectangle [MATH: R,] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f0a1ea7c7a6bbe9b9462a744f63a9458]

Content:
We can describe the entire rectange as [MATH: R = [1,4]\times [2,4],] where [MATH: \times] denotes the Cartesian product.

Content:
Now, let's partition [MATH: R] into [MATH: 6] rectangles of equal area, as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/545bb9800ad27a7a6d0d7a6b3f40a422]

Content:
Note that we can describe our partition without a diagram as follows:

Content:
- The partition of the [MATH: x]-interval [MATH: [1,4]] can be expressed as [MATH: P_1 = \{1,2,3,4\},] where [MATH: x_0=1,] [MATH: x_1=2,] [MATH: x_2=3,] and [MATH: x_3=4.]
- The partition of the [MATH: y]-interval [MATH: [2,4]] can be expressed as [MATH: P_2 = \{2,3,4\},] where [MATH: y_0=2,] [MATH: y_1=3,] and [MATH: y_2=4.]
- The partition of the entire rectangle can be described as [MATH: P = P_1\times P_2.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Calculating a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition

Content:
We have our partition [MATH: P = P_1\times P_2,] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/6faf86c2f1962249a5b41df8627b3b2d]

Content:
Let [MATH: \Delta x_i] be the difference in the [MATH: x]-values of any two successive points in [MATH: P_1 = \{x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3\}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}]

Content:
Similarly, let [MATH: \Delta y_j] be the difference in the [MATH: y]-values of any two successive points in [MATH: P_2= \{y_0, y_1, y_2\}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}]

Content:
It turns out that evaluating double sums over rectangular partitions is important in some parts of higher-level math. For example, how do we compute the sum below?

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j]

Content:
First, note that we can use the product rule for double summations to write this sum as a product of two separate sums:

Content:
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j = \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j]

Content:
Now, recall that for partitions of intervals, the sum of differences in successive points is equal to the length of the interval.

Content:
- Here, the [MATH: x_i]'s partition the interval [MATH: [1,4]] which has length [MATH: 4 - 1 = 3.] So, we have [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^3 \Delta{x}_i = 3.]
- Similarly, the [MATH: y_j]'s partition the interval [MATH: [2,4]] which has length [MATH: 4 - 2 = 2.] So, we have [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^2 \Delta{y}_j = 2.]

Content:
Therefore, we conclude that

Content:
[MATH: ∑_(i = 1)^(m)∑_(j = 1)^(n)Δx_{i}Δy_{j}|= ∑_(i = 1)^(m)Δx_{i} ⋅ ∑_(j = 1)^(n)Δy_{j}; = 3 ⋅ 2; = 6.]

Content:
Note: There is plenty of geometric intuition here.

Content:
- [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i = 3] represents the width of the rectangle, while [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j = 2] represents the height.
- [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n \Delta x_i \Delta y_j] represents the area of the rectangle.

---

Item 3 — Example: Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition

Example Prompt:
Consider the following partitions:

- [MATH: P_1 = \left\{x_0, x_1, \ldots, x_m\right\}] is a partition of the interval [MATH: [-1, 2]]
- [MATH: P_2 = \left\{y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_n\right\}] is a partition of the interval [MATH: [2, 3]]

Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n {3} \Delta x_i \Delta y_j,] where [MATH: \Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}] and [MATH: \Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Using the constant multiple and product rules, we can write the summation as

[MATH: ∑_(i = 1)^(m)∑_(j = 1)^(n)3Δx_{i}Δy_{j}|= 3∑_(i = 1)^(m)∑_(j = 1)^(n)Δx_{i}Δy_{j}; = 3∑_(i = 1)^(m)Δx_{i}∑_(j = 1)^(n)Δy_{j}.]

Note that [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{i=1}^m\Delta x_i] and [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j] are just the lengths of the intervals [MATH: [-1, 2]] and [MATH: [2,3]] respectively. So, we have

[MATH: ∑_(i = 1)^(m)Δx_{i}|= 2 − (− 1) = 3,; ∑_(j = 1)^(n)Δy_{j}|= 3 − 2 = 1.]

Combining our results, we have

[MATH: 3 \sum_{i=1}^m \Delta x_i \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j = 3 \cdot 3 \cdot 1 = 9.]

Item 6 — Example: Computing a Double Sum Over a Rectangular Partition Using a Difference of Squares

Example Prompt:
Consider the following partitions:

- [MATH: P_2 = \left\{y_0, y_1, \ldots, y_n\right\}] is a partition of the interval [MATH: [2, 6]]

Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n (x_i + x_{i-1})\Delta x_i \Delta y_j,] where [MATH: \Delta x_i = x_i - x_{i-1}] and [MATH: \Delta y_j = y_j - y_{j-1}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Using the product rule, we can write the summation as

[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^m (x_i + x_{i-1})\Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n \Delta y_j.]

Note that [MATH: \displaystyle \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j] is just the length of the interval [MATH: [2, 6].] So, we have

[MATH: ∑_(j = 1)^(n)Δy_{j} = 6 − 2 = 4.]

For the sum over [MATH: i,] we can evaluate it as follows:

[MATH: ∑_(i = 1)^(m)(x_{i} + x_{i − 1})Δx_{i}|= (x_{1} + x_{0})Δx_{1} + (x_{2} + x_{1})Δx_{2} + ⋯ + (x_{m} + x_{m − 1})Δx_{n}; = (x_{1} + x_{0})(x_{1} − x_{0}) + (x_{2} + x_{1})(x_{2} − x_{1}) + (x_{m} + x_{m − 1})(x_{m} − x_{m − 1}); = (x_{1}^{2} − x_{0}^{2}) + (x_{2}^{2} − x_{1}^{2}) + ⋯ + (x_{m}^{2} − x_{m − 1}^{2}); = (x_{1}^{2} − x_{0}^{2}) + (x_{2}^{2} − x_{1}^{2}) + ⋯ + (x_{m}^{2} − x_{m − 1}^{2}); = − x_{0}^{2} + x_{m}^{2}; = x_{m}^{2} − x_{0}^{2}; = 6^{2} − 4^{2}; = 20]
Combining our results, we finally arrive at
[MATH: \sum_{i=1}^m (x_i + x_{i-1})\Delta x_i \cdot \sum_{j=1}^n\Delta y_j = 20\cdot 4 = 80.]
